newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Haider backs "Austrians first" job policy.
newsitem.headline: Haider backs "Austrians first" job policy.

text.p: Austrian far right leader Joerg Haider has stirred up a political furore by backing a directive by a regional branch of his Freedom Party to boycott foreign workers.

Haider gave his full support to a ruling on Thursday by Karl-Heinz Grasser, the party's economic spokesman in the southern province of Carinthia, that public building contracts should only go to firms that did not employ foreign workers.

"In a time of high unemployment it is absolutely right to think first of Austrians," Haider said in an interview with current affairs magazine Profil which appears on Monday. "I want to lower the number of foreigners working here."
Social Democrat member of parliament Alfred Gusenbauer slammed Haider's remarks as "unbelievably cynical" and called the far right leader a "notorious troublemaker".
Social Democrat spokesman in Carinthia Michael Ausserwinkler threatened to start investigations against Grasser for abuse of his position and demanded he step down.
Grasser's statement has sparked outrage in Austrian politics and media. Even members of his own party dissociated themselves from his stance.
"I would never issue a directive of that sort because it is simply not legal," said Hubert Gorbach, Freedom Party regional head in the western province of Vorarlberg.
The Chamber of Economy, which represents employers, said the directive had no legal basis and went against every guideline on awarding public orders.
Grasser retreated somewhat on Friday, stressing he had meant firms should make jobs for Austrians a priority.
Haider said the uproar came from employers who were exploiting cheap labour from Slovenia and Croatia. The Carinthian population stood by Grasser 100 percent, he added.
"I told my people that we don't want to play on emotions in this issue. I want to find a solution for the problem of foreigners otherwise there will be an eruption in the population," Haider said.
Unemployment in Carinthia is believed to be around 30,000, in a nation of 300,000 unemployed -- the highest level since World War Two and the founding of the Second Republic.
Workers from Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia are thought to account for 15 to 20 percent of the construction workforce in Carinthia.

Haider has won huge support for his anti-foreigner invective. In a parliamentary debate this month he urged the government of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party to clamp down on immigration and encourage unemployed foreigers to return home.
Haider was forced to resign as governor of Carinthia in 1991 after he praised the labour policies of Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler.

In European Parliament elections last October Haider's Freedom Party won the biggest number of votes in Carinthia. Nationally it is the third strongest party and Europe's biggest far-right parliamentary grouping.
